analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on investment profits by letting taxpayers exclude most long-term capital gains from income.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote at the end of the 101st Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have reinstated a special, lower tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, land, and other assets held for more than a year. Taxpayers could deduct 60% of gains on assets held three years or longer, and 40% of gains on assets held one to three years. It also cut the top tax rate on corporate capital gains from 34% to 28%, and included relief for insolvent farmers who lose farmland to creditors. The 1986 tax overhaul had eliminated the capital gains preference; this bill would have brought much of it back.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations that realize capital gains — overwhelmingly higher-income investors who own stocks, real estate, and business assets. A long-term investor in the top bracket would pay tax on only 40% of a gain on an asset held three years or more. Corporations would see their capital gains rate drop from 34% to 28%. Distressed farmers would get relief from tax on debt-cancellation income when creditors take farmland.

how_it_helps.text: Allows noncorporate taxpayers to deduct 60% of net capital gains on assets held at least three years, and 40% of gains on assets held one to three years, from gross income.
Reduces the alternative tax rate on net capital gains realized by corporations from 34% to 28%.
Provides a special rule so that insolvent farmers who transfer farmland to creditors or sell under threat of foreclosure do not face the capital gains tax preference as an additional tax hit.
Prevents the new capital gains deduction from triggering the alternative minimum tax for principal-residence sales.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, through reduced tax collections on investment income. Because capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households, the foregone revenue would otherwise have been paid largely by the wealthiest taxpayers, and the revenue loss would have to be made up by other taxpayers or by borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The tax preference flows overwhelmingly to households with large capital gains, which are concentrated at the top of the income distribution, so the biggest cuts go to the highest earners.

The bill partially unwinds the 1986 tax overhaul's core bargain — lower rates in exchange for taxing gains as ordinary income — narrowing the tax base and adding back complexity, including a two-tier holding-period structure that creates incentives to time asset sales.
The revenue loss would add to the federal deficit or require offsetting taxes elsewhere, including on wage income that gets no comparable preference.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers facing foreclosure and for a narrow band of long-term holders, the bill offered real relief. But its main effect was a large tax cut on investment income, concentrated among the wealthiest households and corporations, paid for out of federal revenue. It was badly aligned with the 1986 reform's stated goal of taxing all income alike, and the two-tier holding-period rules added complexity back into the code.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Boschwitz introduced the bill on February 9, 1989, with five other senators as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was taken — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill would have cut taxes mainly on capital gains held by wealthier households and corporations, the public interest in a broader, simpler tax base was preserved by its death; the Treasury kept collecting full rates on investment gains. Its backers — and the investors who would have paid lower rates — are the ones left worse off.

for.name: Sen. Rudy Boschwitz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the capital gains tax differential and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 5 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Kasten, Symms, Garn, and Lugar among the original cosponsors, plus two Democratic cosponsors).

for.name: 2 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Cranston as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The seven cosponsors split 5 Republicans and 2 Democrats, but the bill never progressed far enough for a partisan floor fight, so the party alignment of the full Senate is unknown.

industries.industry: Investors in stocks, real estate, and business assets
industries.note: The bill would let them exclude 40-60% of long-term gains from taxable income. Because capital gains concentrate among high-income households, the tax cut's benefits and the foregone revenue come largely at the public's expense.
The corporate alternative capital gains rate would drop from 34% to 28%, cutting corporate tax on gains by about six points.
A special rule would spare insolvent farmers the alternative minimum tax hit on debt-cancellation income when farmland is transferred to creditors or sold under foreclosure threat.
